Method: January–June active machine-days: $248,905,219.25 wagers − $225,267,064.15 payouts = $23,638,155.10 actual house win. Expected house win (theo) is $23,545,364.48. Weighted hold = total house win / total wagers = 9.50%.
Alternative explanation: Wagers include recycled winnings. Actual and expected house win are before operating costs, not net business profit. Reconciliation establishes arithmetic consistency, not accuracy of every source measurement.
Decision implication: Use consistent units and weighted ratios when comparing actual and expected results. Visible in Decision Center; fixed six-month totals here.

Claim: C2. Low total earnings do not establish true underperformance.
Evidence: data/machines.parquet; data/machine_daily.parquet; data/daily_variance.parquet; app.py: build_machine_summary, machine_category.
Method: 55,092 active rows out of 56,110 machine-days. M-5076 has 49 active days, M-1118 has 55 and M-1120 has 132. Compare availability, expected earnings per available hour, exposure and actual-minus-expected payout variation.
Alternative explanation: Short exposure, lifecycle changes, downtime, low demand and payout luck can all lower totals. Peer comparisons do not fully control location or guest mix. Retired machines are not July replacement targets.
Decision implication: Investigate before replacing the bottom ten. Investigate recomputes selected-period evidence; full-period inspection screening is suppressed for restricted date ranges.

Claim: C3. M-1158 is an inspection lead, not a proven faulty machine.
Method: January–June actual house win $15,796.25 versus theo $51,961.00: gap −$36,164.75, modeled standardized gap −4.57, downtime 3.01 hours. The selected June-only standardized gap is about −0.98.
Alternative explanation: The standardized score assumes correct game math and modeled payout variance; it is not a defect probability. Random variation or recording/configuration error remain possible. Screening many machines is not corrected for multiple comparisons.
Decision implication: Inspect paytable/configuration and meter history before spending on replacement. Do not apply the six-month anomaly score to a one-month selection. Inspect the machine evidence in Investigate.

Claim: C4. Demand per available machine-hour softened after February.
Evidence: data/analysis_results.json: monthly, zone_monthly, event_associations; data/property_daily.parquet; analysis/pipeline.py.
Method: Monthly total wagers / total available machine-hours declined from $197.07 in February to $179.67 in June, about 8.8%. Zone and event comparisons provide descriptive context.
Alternative explanation: Seasonality, events, machine mix, location and guest mix overlap. Associations and descriptive before/after movement comparisons do not establish a causal explanation. External context is not a causal control.
Decision implication: Investigate demand patterns before attributing low earnings to hardware. Decision Center and Investigate show selected-period context; the February–June comparison here is fixed.

Claim: C5. Downtime creates estimated missed-play opportunity, not measured net floor loss.
Method: January–June downtime is 5,021.08 hours. Same-machine/weekday operating-rate quantiles, with fallbacks, imply midpoint missed wagers $990,374.55, sensitivity $856,353.76–$1,138,230.52, and midpoint missed theo $92,253.68.
Alternative explanation: Visitors may switch machines, and downtime may fall in quiet hours. Quantile-based low/mid/high estimates are sensitivity cases, not statistical confidence intervals or guaranteed recoverable revenue.
Decision implication: Use monthly/daily availability evidence in Investigate to prioritize investigation. Evaluate maintenance using recovered availability and total-floor contribution, including displacement.

Claim: C6. Tracked-player totals cover only part of casino play.
Evidence: data/analysis_results.json: players; data/guest_groups.parquet; analysis/pipeline.py: player aggregation.
Method: Six-month totals: 113,890 distinct tracked players, $163,804,869.65 wagers, $148,219,409.05 payouts and −$15,585,460.60 player net. Tracked wagers cover 65.81% of machine wagers; 13.61% of tracked players finished ahead.
Alternative explanation: Card users do not represent all visitors. Guest-page counts are player-months and cannot be summed into distinct six-month players. Partial date selections use complete included months, as disclosed in the UI.
Decision implication: Use Guest & Loyalty Insights for monthly group comparisons. Distinct-player, coverage and ahead-share figures above are fixed report findings, not dynamically filtered guest-page cards.

Claim: C7. Tracked wagers and positive player losses are concentrated.
Method: Rank six-month totals by player: the top 1% (1,139 players) by wagers account for 22.86% of tracked wagers. A separate ranking by positive player loss accounts for 19.86% of positive losses.
Alternative explanation: These rankings need not contain the same people. Positive-loss share is not share of net casino win. Region/age group shares on the guest page do not answer individual concentration.
Decision implication: These fixed report findings are available in this appendix and its CSV; the current guest page has no individual concentration cards. Do not use loss concentration to target heavy losers.

Claim: C8. Comp redemption economics changed around May.
Evidence: data/analysis_results.json: loyalty; data/property_daily.parquet; analysis/pipeline.py: loyalty-ledger reconciliation.
Method: January–June economic comp cost is $190,669.30. Weighted redeemed points per face-value dollar fell from 12.51 in April to 5.84 in May and 5.71 in June. Ledger aggregation uses the Las Vegas 6 a.m. gaming-day boundary.
Alternative explanation: A change in redemption mix can alter the ratio without a uniform posted policy change. Face value differs from economic cost. Avoid subtracting comp costs twice when already included in a cost measure.
Decision implication: Investigate policy and redemption mix before claiming cause or loyalty-program ROI. Guest & Loyalty Insights shows monthly comparisons; evaluate changes using a controlled pilot.

Claim: C9. The original property-level forecast beats a constant comparator in May–June.
Evidence: data/analysis_results.json: forecast; analysis/pipeline.py: property forecast; app.py: July Demand Outlook headline metrics.
Method: Fit January–April; compare predictions with May–June floor-wide daily wagers. Weekday MAE is $68,698.55 versus $218,258.10 constant MAE (68.52% lower). January–June refit gives a July 1–30 wager scenario of $40,711,161.62.
Alternative explanation: May–June errors also select the winning method, so this is not an untouched final test of an independently selected winner. July has no actual outcomes. The adjacent April-selection explanation describes a different model (C10).
Decision implication: Label these as the original property-level results. Do not pair their 68.52% improvement with the newer model’s selection protocol or interpret the July scenario as validated realized demand.

Claim: C10. The newer machine-level model has a separate validation protocol.
Method: Fit January–March, select on April, refit January–April, freeze May–June predictions. Machine-day MAE $934.98 versus $1,121.28 baseline (16.6% lower), WAPE 21.24%. Retained floor aggregation gives MAE $99,117.16 versus $231,842.16 and illustrative band coverage 62.3%.
Alternative explanation: These are not C9’s model or error scale. April selects the model and calibrates 10th–90th percentile bands; 62.3% coverage is below nominal 80%. Active roster is supplied; one unseen test machine uses a fallback. No July actuals exist.
Decision implication: Use the saved machine diagnostics separately from the original headline forecast. The current July diagnostic chart incorrectly turns missing actuals into zeros; disregard that Observed series until corrected.

Claim: C11. The current floor view is a bank-level schematic.
Evidence: data/floor_locations.parquet; data/floor_walkways.parquet; data/placements.parquet; app.py: build_location_lookup and selected-period bank summaries.
Method: Supplied bank coordinates locate bank aggregates. Selected-period machine evidence uses dominant bank/zone metadata; placement history supports descriptive movement comparisons.
Alternative explanation: This is not the earlier dated, slot-level occupancy simulator. It does not demonstrate executed moves, movement uplift, or validated power/accessibility/capacity feasibility. Historical bank membership is not necessarily July placement.
Decision implication: Use the map to locate patterns and choose an investigation target. Do not claim 308 occupied slots, six empty slots, animated machine moves or causal location effects from the current visible map.

Claim: C12. Preserve Budget ranks first in the stored, limited Monte Carlo comparison.
Evidence: data/analysis_results.json: simulation; data/scenario_net.npz; analysis/pipeline.py: candidate effects and portfolio enumeration.
Method: 1,000 scenarios, seed 20251107, nine spending candidates and 42 feasible portfolios. At most three action types and $100,000 catalogue cash budget. Keep-budget incremental net is $0; all spending candidates have negative modeled means. Next-best single candidate is comp-policy change at −$1,028.37 mean.
Alternative explanation: Effects and retained-play fractions are assumptions, not measured intervention outcomes. The shortlist is not exhaustive; inspection information value is unpriced. These saved results do not rerun when dates or sandbox controls change.
Decision implication: For the stated 30-day objective, preserve funds under the stored assumptions; consider a separately justified learning action. July Action Plan displays this original comparison, not a live DecisionEngine optimization.

Claim: C13. The interactive action sandbox is a separate what-if calculation.
Evidence: app.py: estimate_action_sandbox, plan_budget_used, add_to_plan; data/analysis_results.json: action_catalog.
Method: Selected historical rates, catalogue prices/lead times and user assumptions produce low/base/high contribution estimates. Planned downtime is deducted from economic benefit. Custom tray actions do not join the stored 42-portfolio ranking.
Alternative explanation: The ranges are sensitivities, not Monte Carlo confidence intervals. The tray currently counts downtime opportunity against cash budget. Its comp-policy estimate omits the original simulation’s demand-loss penalty. Successive action selections also reset in an automated interaction check.
Decision implication: Verify the selected action and compute cash budget separately before acting. M-1158 inspection costs $1,200 cash plus $23.95 opportunity cost; correct cash remaining is $98,800, although the tray reports about $98,776.

Claim: C14. Evaluation plans are proposed; no intervention effect has been measured.
Evidence: app.py: action measurement plans; analysis/pipeline.py; notebooks/01_data_checks.ipynb; this appendix’s evaluation table.
Method: Predefine target, untreated comparison, timing, cash cost and a contribution/availability outcome. Monitor whole-floor play for displacement and inspect meter/configuration evidence for anomalies.
Alternative explanation: No randomized action trial, verified repair effect or July intervention outcome exists in these exports. Thirty days may be underpowered. A favorable simulated result is not proof that an intervention works.
Decision implication: Use the dashboard to choose and design a test, then evaluate genuinely new evidence. Databricks supports the notebook/analysis provenance; the dashboard reads local exports and has no live Databricks or Gemini API connection.
